analysis.title: Agents, Aircons, Allshoring: All Not Priced In
key_insights: Morgan Stanley raises its global power consumption growth forecast by 10% to about 36tn units by 2030, a 4.2% CAGR over 2025-30. It says this is about 15% faster than Street estimates and about 60bps above the IEA. Data centers and fabs drove the last three years of upgrades. Industry (allshoring) and household space cooling now broaden the story.

The Three A's (Agentic AI, Allshoring, Aircons) are the thesis. Powering everything is estimated to unlock about US$0.5trn of market cap by 2027 and lift Street 2028e EPS by about 14% for the preferred names. Powering AI has already added about US$1trn of market cap across the supply chain since 2024.

Pricing power is shifting to power generators and grid operators. Merchant power spreads are expected to expand about 15% by 2028e. Equipment suppliers face pushback from consumers and policymakers after two years of cost inflation, so Morgan Stanley is selective on them. Asian wholesale power prices are up about 20% in the last year.

Equities discount power consumption growth at about a third below the Morgan Stanley base case, close to mid-cycle consumption levels of the past decade. Asia powering-AI names have de-rated YTD even as two-year forward earnings revisions keep rising. Renewable generators have started to re-rate globally.

The report names 36 winners across dependable generators, gas pipeline operators, grid companies and storage suppliers. Winners listed: EDP, RWE, Gulf Development, Keppel, Adani Power, Yangtze Power, Samsung SDI, Hokkaido Electric, Bloom Energy and Solaris Energy. Names to avoid: KEPCO, Tata Power, Global Power Synergy, Huaneng Power, Electric Power Development, Enagas and SNAM.

Agents drive a 1.6x rise in global power consumption by 2030. Agentic workloads are already about 64% of enterprise output tokens. Cost per token is falling but cost per task rises because each task needs many more tokens and model calls. Morgan Stanley's US Internet team forecasts agents as a US$30trn annual market until 2029.

Industry is the largest driver of incremental power demand and cooling alone adds more demand than data center growth through 2030. In Asia, industry is about 43% of incremental electricity demand, roughly 2.7x data centers. Data centers are about 16% of Asia's power-demand growth. China and India account for about 97% of incremental industrial demand to 2030.

Space cooling electricity use is forecast to rise from about 2.9trn units in 2025 to about 4.1trn units by 2030, about a 7% CAGR. Cooling is about 10% of global electricity use but about 30% of peak demand per the IEA. It adds about 40bps to Asia power-demand growth and could match incremental data center demand.

Asia is expected to need 84GW of data center compute by 2030 and to absorb about 15GW of US spillover (Malaysia 4.0GW, Rest of ASEAN 4.0GW, Australia 2.0GW, Japan 1.5GW, India and others 3.6GW). Asia's incremental power consumption is about 4x the US over 2025-30. Asia is about 64% of global incremental power demand.

The US faces a 70GW data center power shortfall before time-to-power solutions and a net 43GW through 2028 (38% of demand), rising to a cumulative 80GW in 2029. Asian spillover cannot cover it. Labor availability and political pushback on data centers are the main constraints on behind-the-meter additions. Morgan Stanley favors onsite power providers BE, INIO and SEI.

In the US, Morgan Stanley is Overweight SRE and AEP for transmission investment (advanced-stage load pipelines of about 127GW and about 69GW). NEE and VST are favored for integrated data center platforms. NEE targets 15GW of originated data center capacity by 2035 with upside to 30GW. VST launched the Helix Digital Infrastructure venture with KKR, Kuwait Investment Authority and NVIDIA.

Hyperscaler returns are insensitive to power cost. A 17% rise in power prices from US$120/MWh to US$140/MWh costs only about 60bp of ROE, and ROE stays above 30% even at about US$160/MWh. A 20% change in power prices moves earnings only about 1%. This gives utilities room to charge data centers higher tariffs that help fund grid capex.

Fuel mix is shifting toward dependable power. Fossil fuels are about 50% of the global mix by 2030. Asia adds about 303GW of coal, 61GW of gas and 51GW of nuclear through 2030, plus more than 2TW of renewables. Data centers could underwrite about 20mntpa of LNG imports into Asia by 2030, about one fifth of new US shale LNG exports. Gas midstream earnings are expected to inflect.

Grid investment is rising. Asia needs about US$1trn of grid investment through 2030, and global utility capex stays about 2x 2019 levels through 2029e. Duck curves are reshaping into double-humped camels in India and Thailand's evening peak is rising with EV charging. Batteries gain value but saturate quickly in Australia, where Morgan Stanley sees battery deployment approaching saturation in the merchant market.

Behind-the-meter power is a growing theme. Demand is estimated at 8GW in Asia and 47GW in the US by 2030. Gulf Development, Adani Power and Sembcorp supply data centers behind the meter. Australia, Malaysia and Thailand encourage 'bring your own power' requirements. US reshoring could add up to 113GW of electricity capacity need through 2035 in a scenario where the US reaches 20% of global manufacturing by 2050.

Europe's power demand is inflecting after years of decline, with 2.2% CAGR forecast over 2026-30. Data centers add about 90TWh over 2025-30. Preferred plays: National Grid, SSE, E.ON and Elia for grids, Engie and RWE for flexible generation, RWE and EDP for data centers. Powered-land deals are a monetization lever, with RWE holding 3GW of available capacity.

China is not a US-style power shortage trade. Demand is forecast to grow about 5% CAGR and Morgan Stanley prefers defensive, low-cost generators. Yangtze Power is the most preferred stock (Overweight, PT Rmb34.98, 18.9x 2027e P/E, 3.8% dividend yield).

KEPCO is Underweight on weak 2Q26 results, constrained tariff flexibility and leverage. Debt is W211tn as of 2Q26, and Samsung Electronics and SK hynix reportedly rejected a proposal to prepay W25tn of electricity bills over five years. Samsung SDI is Overweight on energy storage and data center backup power demand.

sector_views.rationale: Pricing power and spreads expand about 15% by 2028e as consumption outpaces supply. Fossil-led generation is a bottleneck as nuclear is inflexible and batteries deflate merchant renewable economics.

Access to power grids is critical, which should re-rate distribution and transmission equities. Asia needs about US$1trn of grid investment through 2030. Some Asian and European grid names are on the avoid list.
Earnings expected to inflect on LNG demand from data centers, but the Japanese and Indian pipeline names are rated Equal-weight and Enagas and SNAM are Underweight.
Selective, as pricing power shifts to infrastructure owners and equipment multiples have corrected. Onsite power names BE, INIO and SEI are the exceptions.
Renewables and storage are pricing in a lot of growth already. Battery deployment compresses merchant arbitrage returns, though capacity payments support storage.

trade_ideas.description: Long onsite and behind-the-meter power providers BE, INIO and SEI (all Overweight)
trade_ideas.rationale: The US faces a 43GW net data center power shortfall through 2028, so any provider with a path to supply power in 2027-28 should secure attractive agreements.
trade_ideas.risk: Labor availability and political pushback on data centers limit behind-the-meter additions.

trade_ideas.description: Long US grid and transmission utilities SRE and AEP (both Overweight)
trade_ideas.rationale: Largest advanced-stage load pipelines in coverage, about 127GW and about 69GW, with transmission capex embedded in plans and potential upside.

trade_ideas.description: Long US data center platform utilities NEE and VST (both Overweight)
trade_ideas.rationale: Integrated platforms (NEE data center hubs, VST Helix venture) shorten time to power and give a competitive edge in winning load.

trade_ideas.description: Own the 36 power infrastructure winners and avoid KEPCO, Tata Power, Global Power Synergy, Huaneng, Electric Power Development, Enagas and SNAM
trade_ideas.rationale: Power spreads widen about 15% by 2028e and generators and grid owners gain pricing power while equipment suppliers face pushback.
trade_ideas.risk: Regulatory headwinds on data centers and consumer power bills, and battery saturation in merchant markets.

risk_factors: Regulatory headwinds as policymakers tighten rules on data centers and consumers face rising power bills.
Equipment cost inflation and consumer or policymaker pushback on prices.
Labor availability (CSIS estimates the US needs 140,000 more skilled tradespeople by 2030) and permitting limits on gas and behind-the-meter additions.
Political and public pushback on data centers, including moratoriums.
Battery saturation and overbuild for flat load shapes in merchant markets such as Australia.
Tariff and funding constraints, for example KEPCO's leverage and politically sensitive tariff hikes in Korea.
Geopolitical instability in the Middle East and LNG supply disruptions.
Spillover capacity outside the US may not be enough to absorb the US power shortfall.
Regulatory uncertainty in Spain over data center sustainability requirements.
Morgan Stanley discloses that it does business with the companies it covers, which may be a conflict of interest.
charts_described: Exhibit 17 compares Morgan Stanley's 2025-30 global power demand CAGR of 4.2% with the IEA's, about 60bps lower.
Exhibit 18 bridges global power demand from 29,654bn units in 2025 to 36,346bn units in 2030e, with industrial adding 2,279bn, residential 1,760bn, data centers 1,712bn and commercial 941bn.
Exhibit 21 bridges global incremental power demand 2025-30 with China adding 2,984bn units and Asia ex-China 1,272bn units, about 64% of the total.
Exhibit 44 walks the US shortfall from 116GW of demand through 25GW of data centers under construction and 21GW of grid access to a 70GW gap, and then to 43GW after time-to-power solutions.
Exhibit 48 shows incremental Asia power demand 2025-30 with industrial adding 1,912bn units, residential 890bn, commercial 784bn and data centers 670bn.
Exhibit 33 shows hyperscaler ROE of 33.6% at US$100/MWh and US$34.0 per million output tokens, declining to 30.2% at US$170/MWh.
vol_and_positioning: Equities are discounting power consumption growth at about a third below the Morgan Stanley base case, close to mid-cycle levels of the past decade.
Asia powering-AI beneficiaries have de-rated YTD on P/B despite continued earnings revisions.
Global renewable power generators have started to re-rate on P/B as investors price in a more diversified energy mix, narrowing the fossil discount.
Gas and power utilities with grid exposure in Asia outperformed benchmarks in 2026 but are still de-rated YTD.
geopolitical: The energy shock linked to the Iran conflict and LNG disruptions pushed policymakers toward energy security, reliability and domestic resilience. The report cites this as a driver of Europe's AccelerateEU electrification plan and a new capex cycle in Asia.
Global conflict keeps LNG costs high versus alternative fuels, which the report says the market is not ready to price into gas midstream earnings.
Middle East data center expansion faces geopolitical instability, with an AWS data center affected by Iran strikes cited as an example.
China hyperscalers plan to grow 2-3GW of capacity outside China annually, and Thailand is seeing China hyperscalers underwrite capacity.
Growing US political pushback on data centers, including moratoriums, is a headwind to behind-the-meter buildout.

tension_points.bull_case: Time-to-power solutions (behind-the-meter turbines and engines, Bloom fuel cells, nuclear sites) cut the US shortfall from 70GW to 43GW through 2028. Asia can absorb about 15GW of spillover and Utilities team tracks 25-30GW of manufacturer orders for 2026-28.
tension_points.bear_case: Labor availability and political pushback on data centers limit buildout. Rest-of-world capacity is not enough to absorb the US shortfall, and the net gap still reaches 80GW cumulatively in 2029.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A faster behind-the-meter ramp would change the shortfall math. Bringing 30GW of total BTM generation online through 2026-28 would cut the shortfall to 35GW.

tension_points.bull_case: Build now, power later policies and equipment cost inflation (construction costs up about 8% YoY) support higher medium-term wholesale prices, with FY29 base-load futures in contango, favoring AGL and Origin.
tension_points.bear_case: Battery saturation, overbuild for flat load shapes and near-term supply growth of about 4% weigh on FY28 prices year on year, contrary to global market trends.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Battery saturation through overbuild for flat load shapes would undercut the constructive medium-term power price view.
